idiom_name: SwiftUI @State declared private in the highest view that needs the value; @Binding to share it with subviews; @StateObject/@Observable model when it must outlive the view
implementation_notes: SwiftUI provides the colocated cell: @State creates storage managed by the framework for the view that declares it, and Apple's guidance is to declare state as private in the highest view in the hierarchy that needs access to the value, share it with subviews read-only or through a @Binding, and use state only for storage that is local to a view and its subviews - which is this pattern stated in framework terms. The replacement for the classic structure is that view-owned cell plus bindings; the observable-model form (@StateObject, @Observable, the environment) is the deliberate exception for state that spans views without a shared ancestor or must survive the view. Choose the classic shared form when the value genuinely belongs to the app or the document, and keep models out of views that never read them so the update scope stays small.
pitfalls: @State is tied to the view's identity: if the identity changes (a branch in a conditional, a ForEach id, a wrapper view) the storage is discarded and the value resets.

A State property instantiates its default value every time SwiftUI creates the view, so expensive objects or side effects in the default run repeatedly; defer creation to .task and use an optional, as Apple documents.

Sharing by passing a plain value copies it (the subview cannot write back); two-way sharing needs @Binding, and passing both a value and a binding for the same state is the usual source of surprising resets.
